items.stem: Two hospitals cannot exchange a patient's records even though both use electronic systems. The most likely root cause is a lack of:

options.text: Agreed interoperability standards for data exchange
options.rationale: Correct: without shared standards, systems cannot reliably exchange and interpret data.
Storage capacity does not determine whether two systems can interpret each other's data.
Bandwidth is not the barrier when the data formats are not mutually understood.
Staffing levels do not resolve a data-format interoperability problem.

items.explanation: Correct: without shared standards, systems cannot reliably exchange and interpret data.

items.stem: A clinical decision-support system fires so many low-value pop-up alerts that clinicians routinely dismiss them. This problem is known as:

options.rationale: Correct: excessive, low-value alerts cause clinicians to ignore them, a recognised safety risk.
Interoperability concerns data exchange between systems, not alert overload.
Data minimisation is a privacy principle, not the alert-overload phenomenon.
Version control concerns tracking changes, not alert overload.

items.explanation: Correct: excessive, low-value alerts cause clinicians to ignore them, a recognised safety risk.

items.stem: Which TWO are dimensions of data quality in health informatics? (Select TWO)

options.rationale: Correct: accuracy, whether data correctly reflect reality, is a core data-quality dimension.
Correct: completeness, whether required data are present, is a core data-quality dimension.
Bandwidth is a network property, not a data-quality dimension.
Screen resolution is a display property, not a data-quality dimension.

items.explanation: Correct: accuracy, whether data correctly reflect reality, is a core data-quality dimension.
